attempts.raw_response: The whole scheme of redemption through another's suffering appeared to them fundamentally unjust, a moral outrage that violated the very principles of rational justice they held sacred. God, in their view, could not possibly demand an innocent sacrifice for the guilty, nor could He transfer the merits of one being to another, any more than one person's obedience could cancel another's disobedience. For the deist, religion was essentially a matter of natural theology—God's existence and attributes to be discovered through reason alone, without the need for special revelation. The scriptures, while perhaps containing useful moral instruction, were not divinely inspired in any supernatural sense, and the miracles attributed to Christ and the prophets were either exaggerated or entirely fictitious. Their faith was a quiet acknowledgment of a creator who, having established the universe with its immutable laws, remained utterly indifferent to human affairs.

pair.human_continuation:
The name atheism, which, it is true, orthodoxy
held ready for every belief incorrect according to its standard, was on the
contrary undeserved. The deists did not attack Christian revelation, still
less belief in God. They considered the atheist bereft of reason, and they
by no means esteemed historical revelation superfluous. The end of the
latter was to stir the mind to move men to reflection and conversion, to
transform morals, and if anyone declared it unnecessary because it contains
nothing but natural truths, he was referred to the works of Euclid, which
certainly contain nothing which is not founded in the reason, but which no
one but a fool will consider unnecessary in the study of mathematics.
pair.prefix:
It was inevitable that the doctrines of original
sin, of satisfaction and atonement should prove especially objectionable to
the purely rational temper of the deists. Neither the guilt of others (the
sin of our ancestors) nor the atonement of others (Christ's death on the
cross) can be imputed to us; Christ can be called the Savior only by way of
metaphor, only in so far as the example of his death leads us on to faith
and obedience for ourselves.

source_document.title: History Of Modern Philosophy by Richard Falckenberg
